## [2026-10-22](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-22.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [UlaCache: Unified Logical Addressing for Sparse LLM Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29820>)

UlaCache gives sparse-attention histories stable logical addresses across GPU and CPU memory, reducing redundant copies while sharing GPU cache capacity across requests. Its parallel replacement and transfer scheduling let GLM-5.3 sustain larger decode batches under matched memory budgets, reaching up to 2.51× HiSparse’s peak decoding throughput on eight B300 GPUs with speculative decoding enabled.

**Published:** 2026-10-21 · **First seen:** 2026-10-22T10:04:20.486Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Sparse Attention, KV Cache, GPU CPU Memory

**Public availability:** 2026-10-22T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent?show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29820>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Full pinned v1 PDF (12 pages) and HTML methods, evaluation and related work inspected. Stable logical IDs resolve to GPU/CPU storage slots; TP distributes retained history across ranks and uses separate local buffers for selected copies, whereas DP keeps rank-local pools. PB-LRU uses shared recency buckets and hierarchical bitmaps; transfer plans protect current readers, exchange incoming/outgoing KV, and commit address mappings only after transfers finish. Selection-plan reuse and cross-layer prefetch apply when layers share sparse selections. GLM-5.3 uses FP8 weights/KV and BF16 activations on eight H200 or eight B300 GPUs; CPU budgets are128GB or192GB per GPU, respectively, and the B300 persistent model/cache budget is272GB per GPU. Multi-LexSum inputs contain64K–128K tokens and generate2048 greedy output tokens. Under matched memory budgets, peak decode-throughput ratios versus HiSparse with two-step MTP are H200 DP1.16×/TP1.70× and B300 DP1.73×/TP2.51×. This differs from prior RemoteKV (prefill transfer scaling), CacheSmith (RAG reuse selection) and PageWeaver (sparse query unions): the central contribution is active sparse-history placement and replacement. Timing: v1 received2026-10-21T14:46:11Z; the original cs.DC Thursday22 batch and official20:00US/Eastern schedule imply announcement2026-10-22T00:00Z, within this daily window. No verified author implementation link was found in the paper or exact-name public repository lookup.

**Limitations:** One sparse-attention model and two eight-GPU platforms were measured; examples of other architectures are motivation, not their evaluation. All requests finish prefill before measured decoding, and each system’s observed maximum is taken over its own measured batch sizes, so these are decode-only peak-throughput comparisons, not fixed-batch or online end-to-end SLO speedups. At batch1 UlaCache is slower than fully GPU-resident SGLang in all eight configurations, though faster than HiSparse. Bucketed LRU is approximate; its scheduling ablation excludes data transfer and can lose to naive LRU when replacement pressure is low. TP score all-gather, local copied buffers, transfer bandwidth, metadata and workspaces remain costs. No downstream quality study, distributed fault-recovery study or independently reproduced result is claimed; a public UlaCache code release was not verified.

## [2026-10-18](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-18.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22179>)

LCT stores BF16 weights, saved activations and optimizer buffers in a lossless exponent-coded format, using parallel GPU encoding, fused updates and a shared overflow arena for repeated compression during training. The new paper quantifies a memory-versus-step-time trade-off and explains how the format adapts to changing tensor magnitudes, enabling longer tested sequences on a memory-constrained GPU without quantizing the stored BF16 values.

**Published:** 2026-10-15 · **First seen:** 2026-10-18T21:44:21.869Z · **Novelty:** material-update · **Tags:** Lossless Compression, Training Memory, GPU Codecs, BF16

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22179>) · [Code](<https://github.com/Maxzhu123/Losslessly_Compressed_Tensors>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Read methodology4.1-4.7, storage/scale analysis5, experiments6 and relevant AppendicesA-C, including timing/memory accounting and training integration. Bounded Huffman prefixes plus literal escapes compress exponents while preserving sign/fraction bytes; dense matrix products still require reconstruction. On one RTX3090 with PyTorch2.14/Triton3.8, activation compression in162M NanoGPT cuts peak allocated memory16058to12103MiB(24.6%) while optimizer-step time rises8.411to9.013s(7.2%). All-component compression yields11964.6MiB/9.136s, and a3400-step run has similar validation loss. Qwen3-4B-Base full-parameter BF16/Muon memory-time tests at batch1 fit3500tested tokens versus1000for the baseline; at1000, memory is21327.8to16262.4MiB with4.006to4.273s step time. This is a new detailed paper/analysis of older public code, not a new implementation release. The prior README says paper-coming-soon; the complete October12 tree contains only a graphical-abstractPDF, not the paper.

**Limitations:** Storage is lossless for input BF16 bit patterns; converting FP32 to BF16 first still loses information, and this does not prove bitwise-identical whole training. Compression depends on exponent statistics, block padding and overflow; small or mismatched tensors can expand. Requires explicit custom-autograd/operator integration, and compressed weights are not ordinary registered nn.Parameters. Shared-arena sizing must include live replacements/fragmentation. Training time/peak memory use only five measured optimizer steps after three warmups; Qwen tests do not establish long-run fine-tuning quality. Reported memory is PyTorch allocated, not allocator-reserved or all device memory; training includes the entire shared arena. Only BF16 is supported here and GEMMs decode first. Code was inspected but not executed; no independent reproduction.

**Update:** 2026-10-16: The newly announced detailed paper adds bounded-code/scale-shift/storage analysis and controlled codec, NanoGPT and Qwen memory-time evaluations to the earlier public LCT implementation (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.22179v1; https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&amp;show=2000; https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html). The repository was created October4 with code commits through October12; its README still marks the paper coming soon and its inspected pre-window tree has no paperPDF (https://github.com/Maxzhu123/Losslessly\_Compressed\_Tensors; https://api.github.com/repos/Maxzhu123/Losslessly\_Compressed\_Tensors/git/trees/396b9d6fb725956cb0735a83b5de368319d0b823?recursive=1). Commit dates document earlier content, not exact first-public visibility. Preserve October15 as this paper's receipt date; the paper update is inferred as October16T00Z from its original cs.LG batch and official schedule. This is delayed editorial review within the72-hour window, not a claim of newly released code.

## [2026-10-16](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-16.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21500>)

This study explains why a remote key-value cache can be slower than recomputing a prompt, then shards cache work across context-parallel ranks and remote servers while moving loads off the engine's blocking path. Its production-trace replay and bandwidth-plus-fixed-cost model give serving engineers a practical way to decide when cache reuse helps, and to separate capacity benefits from first-token latency.

**Published:** 2026-10-15 · **First seen:** 2026-10-17T10:02:23.724Z · **Novelty:** material-update · **Tags:** Remote KV Cache, Context Parallelism, Asynchronous Loading, Trace Replay

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21500>) · [Code](<https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/5545>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Reviewed Sections 3-8, all tables, the collective-safe sharding protocol and the linked LMCache PR. GLM-5.3 FP8 runs on one 8-GPU B300 PCP8/EP8 prefill engine using vLLM 0.31.0 and LMCache 0.5.5. A 683-request production trace and a primed 450-request subset support the cost model; on the hit-heavy subset, final prefill-leg p99 is 0.67 s versus 83.32 s for the overloaded single-server baseline, with 98.5% of prompt tokens cached. Final remote-hit median remains 0.40 s versus 0.31 s for recomputation. This is a new detailed paper and evaluation of engineering whose sharding PR opened October 8. Public-paper availability is inferred as October 16 00:00 UTC from its primary cs.DC batch and the official announcement schedule; the October 15 receipt date is preserved. The linked PR 5545 implements the synchronous sharding component, not all asynchronous extensions or client fixes evaluated in the paper.

**Limitations:** Each condition ran once; differences below about 10% are not established. The dramatic p99 ratio repairs an overloaded hit-heavy queue rather than showing a universal cache speedup. Replays omit decode handoff and shared multi-engine contention, and the selected subset fits the private cache. The approximately 17K-token crossover is a one-point-fitted prediction, not a measured general threshold. Deployment comparisons change parallelism and placement too. Correctness evidence is needle retrieval and soak testing, not bit-exact or broad answer-quality proof. The linked PR remains open; no independent reproduction was performed. PR 5545 explicitly rejects asynchronous loading; the paper references separate extensions and fixes, so this link is not a complete reproduction artifact.

**Update:** 2026-10-16: The newly announced paper adds a detailed fixed-cost/bandwidth model, collective-safe remote-cache protocol, production-trace evaluation and limitations beyond the earlier sharding implementation (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.21500v1; https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent?skip=0&amp;show=2000; https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html; https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/5545). The PR opened October 8, which is provenance rather than an asserted exact first-public timestamp. The preserved October 15 published\_on is this paper's receipt date, not the implementation's release date.

## [2026-10-15](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-15.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [CacheSmith: Accurate RAG Serving under Latency SLOs with Adaptive KV Reuse](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18925>)

CacheSmith adapts how much cross-chunk attention is recomputed when reusing cached RAG context, jointly choosing request batches and a warm-up, probe and patch plan under latency budgets. Its objective counts responses that meet both a generation-quality gate and a first-token deadline, helping serving systems allocate recomputation where it improves useful responses rather than latency alone.

**Published:** 2026-10-13 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T15:09:52.031Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** RAG, KV Reuse, Selective Recomputation, Latency SLO

**Public availability:** 2026-10-15T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.AR/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18925>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Reviewed method, planner/scheduler Algorithm 1, runtime and all evaluation/ablation sections. vLLM 0.10.2 experiments use Llama 3.1-8B on one 96 GB RTX PRO 6000 and Qwen3-32B on two, EPYC 9554 and NVMe-cached chunks. Across 96 task/arrival/SLO combinations, authors exceed an oracle best-static configuration in 93 and report 2-27.5% higher quality-gated SLO attainment. Timing is inferred from CacheSmith's PRIMARY cs.AR Oct 15 batch plus official announcement schedule; Oct 13 is receipt, not asserted public release.

**Limitations:** Quality is estimated from offline demand profiles, not guaranteed for every request; experiments use four small benchmark-derived/synthetic tasks, Poisson/Gamma arrivals and precomputed SSD chunks. Majority signal selection can hurt minority requests in mixed batches. Query-context baselines share authors' untuned reimplementation because original kernels were unavailable. Quality gates are task-specific, not general answer correctness. No verified implementation release or independent reproduction; do not relabel the paper's 27.5% as percentage points.

## [2026-10-13](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-13.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Ember: Making Unified Virtual Memory Practical for Discrete-Memory GPUs](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13408>)

Ember keeps oversubscribed GPU allocations accessible in host memory and selectively promotes useful regions into GPU memory, with an adaptive variant using hardware access counters and proactive reclamation. This reduces page-migration thrashing when model weights exceed device capacity, offering a concrete memory-management design for constrained LLM inference rather than requiring the whole model to fit on the GPU.

Sections 4–8 distinguish stock-CUDA static placement from the patched-driver adaptive policy. Section 7.4 tests Qwen2.5-14B/Qwen3-32B generation on RTX 5080, A40 and H200, each capped to 16 GB; at 1.41x oversubscription, the static variant reports 4.7–13x over stock UVM.

**Limitations:** These are 128-token decode benchmarks, not serving throughput: no strategy exceeds 3 tokens/s in the oversubscribed cases. Adaptive placement requires a driver patch and administrator access; only managed allocations and one GPU-to-host tier are controlled. ## [2026-10-13](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-13.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [SlackSwap: Bandwidth-Aware Activation Swapping and Recomputation for Memory-Efficient DNN Training](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13003>)

SlackSwap treats host-link time as a limited budget, offloading activations that would be expensive to rebuild and recomputing cheaper tensors once that transfer budget is exhausted. Its trace-driven simulations suggest that combining bandwidth-aware placement with asynchronous copies can retain training throughput under tight activation-memory budgets, while leaving real-system performance to be demonstrated.

**Published:** 2026-10-09 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:36:42.817Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Activation Memory, Offloading, Recomputation

**Public availability:** 2026-10-12T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent?skip=50&show=100>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13003>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Delayed discovery of the verified October 12 batch; original October 9 submission retained and availability inferred from the dated listing plus schedule. Algorithm 1 and Sections 3–4 specify two-pass planning, FIFO offloads and earliest-deadline-first prefetches. A100 simulations of BERT-Large, GPT-2 XL and a Llama-7B-style model retain 96.3–99.6% of unlimited-memory throughput at half the activation budget, 1.10–1.11x the best simulated baseline.

**Limitations:** All performance results are simulated. The model omits allocator fragmentation, copy-induced HBM contention, and shared PCIe/host-memory contention; model states remain resident on one GPU. The SwapAdvisor comparison omits its operator-order and memory-pool genetic search. No dedicated implementation or independent reproduction was verified.

### [ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13778>)

ReplaySSM represents recurrent state as a checkpoint plus recent inputs, avoiding most full-state writes and making speculative rollback a buffer operation. The new paper extends this approach with separate precisions for output reads and recurrent updates, reducing the feedback of state-quantization error during long generations.

**Published:** 2026-10-09 · **First seen:** 2026-10-12T10:04:28Z · **Novelty:** material-update · **Tags:** SSM State, Speculative Decoding, Low Precision

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13778>) · [Blog](<https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/>) · [Code](<https://github.com/Johnny-Liou/ReplaySSM>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. The new quantization study reports mean GPQA-Diamond losses of 13.05 percentage points for shared NVFP4+SR versus 2.36 for NVFP4 reads with FP16+SR recurrence across four hybrid models. Separately, FP32-state decoding at batch 256 improves whole-step latency by 1.20–1.47× on one H100 or B300 per model.

**Limitations:** Quantization accuracy uses emulation, standard decoding and full-precision prefill; residual errors remain. Performance gains shrink at batch 1. The public fork contains experimental paths beyond the upstream Mamba2 integration; benchmarks were not reproduced.

**Update:** 2026-10-12: the newly announced paper adds two-precision state algorithms and long-generation KL/accuracy experiments beyond the June 15 ReplaySSM blog (https://dao-lab.ai/blog/). ### [PageWeaver: KV-Guided Query Unions for Sparse Attention](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11201>)

PageWeaver groups sparse-attention queries by overlap in their selected KV pages, then executes them through a kernel that retains each query's original support and output location. This reduces repeated page traversal while accounting for the cost of constructing useful query groups.

### [RaReCache: Bridging the Gap in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse via Rank disagreement-based Selective Recomputation](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11358>)

RaReCache maps an existing smaller model's KV cache into a larger model and ranks token positions using disagreement between full-rank and reduced-rank predictions. Recomputing only the selected positions lets the larger model recover part of the quality lost by cache mapping while avoiding a complete target-model prefill.

### [MOLT: A Fine-Grained GPU Memory Sharing System for LLM Serving with Opportunistic Fine-Tuning](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05748>)

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash combines cross-layer cache reuse, sparse attention, FP4 KV storage, and approximate replay of sliding-window states to shrink long-context memory. **Evidence:** technical-report; full-text. The report explains cache layout and replay mechanics and reports 890 bytes per token for global GPU-resident KV, roughly one quarter of DeepSeek-V4-Flash, with persistent cache around one eighth of that baseline.
